Subject: Request: sizing for Dedicated run (Velocera)

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — Velocera is excited about the latency profile Redwood showed. Were starting procurement planning and need a baseline sizing recommendation for a Dedicated deployment. High-level workload notes (attached csv with raw sampling):
- Monthly active users (MAU): ~200k
- Average requests/day: ~6M (peak burst factor ~6x)
- Typical prompt footprint: 120 tokens input; generation ~350 tokens average
- Expected steady-state concurrency (business hours, US): ~120 QPS across the fleet; peak burst observed in tests: ~700 QPS for ~3-7 minutes
- p95 tail latency target for generation: <= 350ms (token streaming acceptable, but first-token p95 matters)
- SLO target: 99.9% for inference success and p95 latency, with an ops window for graceful degradation to cheaper model variants

Questions for Redwood: can you map this to tokens/sec and recommended GPU slab sizing for a Dedicated pool? Were interested in a cost-aware design: a lower-cost quantized 7B as primary plus a 13B fallback for higher quality queries. Important outputs we need: tokens/sec per GPU (7B q4 and 13B q8-ish), expected p95 latency at those loads, recommended headroom percentage (for bursts and cache cold starts), and a short Mutual Action Plan so procurement can line up approvals.

Also looping in Legal for procurement cadence.

Thanks — happy to hop on a quick sizing call if that helps.

— Alex
Ops / Velocera

Alex — thanks for the detail and the CSV. Quick read-through and a first-pass sizing framework below (Ill attach a short spreadsheet with the math). Quoting your key ask so were aligned.

On 2028-06-24 at 09:12 Alex Morozov wrote:
> Typical prompt footprint: 120 tokens input; generation ~350 tokens average
> Expected steady-state concurrency (business hours, US): ~120 QPS; peak ~700 QPS
> p95 target <= 350ms; SLO 99.9%

Summary (first-pass):
- Tokens per request (avg): 470 tokens (input + output)
- Steady-state tokens/sec = 120 QPS * 470 = 56,400 tokens/sec
- Peak tokens/sec = 700 QPS * 470 = 329,000 tokens/sec

Performance assumptions (Redwood runtime, tuned kernels, KV cache warm for repeated prefixes):
- 7B quantized (q4/avx-like path) on a single 80GB-class GPU (A100 / H100 class perf) -> conservative sustained ~6,500 tokens/sec (single-stream amortized with batching up to 8). p95 first-token latency estimate ~120-180ms at moderate batching; tail rises with concurrency if KV cold.
- 13B quantized (q8-ish) -> ~2,400 tokens/sec; first-token p95 ~180-300ms under similar batching assumptions.

Sizing calc (no headroom):
- Steady: 56,400 / 6,500 ≈ 8.7 -> 9 GPUs (7B primary)
- Peak: 329,000 / 6,500 ≈ 50.6 -> 51 GPUs (if all handled by 7B)

Recommended production design (cost & reliability balanced):
1) Primary pool: 12x 7B-quant GPUs (covers steady-state + ~35% headroom). Rationale: 9 GPUs math + 35% cushion for cache cold, warmup and background ops = ~12. This keeps p95 latencies inside target for most traffic and lets us maintain SLO with graceful degradation.
2) Burst/fallback pool: 10x 13B-quant GPUs as overflow for quality-critical paths (use routing policy: price-sensitive queries → 7B; quality-critical or latched flows → 13B during heavy loads). This prevents desaturation of the 7B pool during sustained peaks.
3) Autoscaling policy: allow short-duration burst to spin up +25% additional GPUs for up to 10 minutes; persistent >10min triggers escalation and temporary throttling policies.

Operational notes: prefix/KV caching reduces effective tokens/sec by ~10-25% on repeat prompts — we include that in the attached spreadsheet as scenario A/B. Cold-cache periods (region failover or restarts) require the headroom cushion.

Ill let Ben add the risk buffer numbers and a run-of-the-mill cost delta. Proposed next step: 30-minute technical sizing call tomorrow where we walk the precise traffic traces and mark leader vs follower routes.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference
Attachment: redwood_dedicated_proposal_v1.pdf (proposal summary, 110KB)

From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Request: sizing for Dedicated run (Velocera)

Alex / team — adding a short scenario table and headroom policy so procurement can see clear options. I pulled the CSV and replayed a short synthetic burst with your sampled distribution. Numbers below are conservative (we bias for tail-resilience).

Scenario | Effective tokens/sec required | GPU type | GPUs needed (raw) | GPUs recommended (with headroom)
Light baseline (off-hours) | 18,000 | 7B-q4 | 18,000/6,500 ≈ 3 | 4 (25% headroom)
Business steady | 56,400 | 7B-q4 | ≈ 9 | 12 (35% headroom + cache churn)
Peak short burst | 329,000 | mix: 7B primary + 13B fallback | if 100% 7B -> 51 | Recommended: 30x7B + 20x13B (burst orchestration)
Sustained peak ( > 15 min ) | 200,000 (degraded routing) | 13B-q8 for quality routes | 200,000/2,400 ≈ 84 | Operationally: cap at 40x13B + throttling and spool backoff

Key trade-offs and mitigations:
- Latency: first-token p95 is most sensitive to model cold start and KV misses. Warmed caches and sticky routing reduce p95 by ~30-50ms.
- Cost: running pure 7B slab to cover absolute peak is cost-prohibitive; recommended hybrid approach to meet p95 SLO while keeping committed spend reasonable.
- Headroom policy: we recommend committed slab = steady-state recommendation + 35% buffer. Burst capacity can be negotiated as a short-term autoscale pool (reserve convertible to committed capacity after 30 days if utilization remains).

Mutual Action Plan (high level):
1) Technical deep-dive (tomorrow) — confirm traffic slices and critical routes (Priyom to run a short model-run trace).
2) Legal/Proc review — Redwood to provide draft MSA + pricing delta for reserved slab (Kimberly + Legal loop).
3) Pilot in Dedicated: 6-week test with monitoring and rollback policies (Redwood provides observability dashboards and alerting).

Links: HubSpot deal [VEL-2028-042] and a short spreadsheet linked in the Drive.

Ben Carter
Head of Dedicated Solutions — Redwood Inference
